overrides.content:
name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint
      - run: pnpm format:check
      - run: pnpm typecheck
      - run: pnpm test

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      # Plain Next.js build: proves the app is portable beyond Cloudflare.
      - run: pnpm build

  cloudflare:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm cf:build
      - run: pnpm cf:size
      # The Linux-built OpenNext output, deployed by hand to the test shop Worker with
      # `wrangler deploy --env test` (docs/DEPLOYMENT.md, "Test shop"). Contains no secrets:
      # CI has none, and secrets are bound to the Worker at runtime.
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: open-next-build
          path: .open-next
          include-hidden-files: true
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 7
      # Run the built Worker in workerd (the Cloudflare runtime) and smoke-test it, so runtime
      # errors that `next start` cannot show are caught before deployment.
      - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - name: Start Worker locally
        run: |
          pnpm exec wrangler dev --ip 127.0.0.1 --port 8787 > wrangler-dev.log 2>&1 &
          for i in $(seq 1 90); do
            curl -s -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8787/robots.txt && exit 0
            sleep 1
          done
          echo "Worker did not start"; cat wrangler-dev.log; exit 1
      - name: Smoke-test the Worker
        run: pnpm test:e2e --grep @smoke --project desktop
        env:
          PLAYWRIGHT_BASE_URL: http://127.0.0.1:8787
      - if: always()
        run: cat wrangler-dev.log || true

  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: pnpm build
      - run: pnpm test:e2e
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        if: failure()
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report
          retention-days: 7

  node-standalone:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm build:node
        env:
          INDEXING: "off"
      - name: Relocate the standalone runtime outside the checkout
        run: node scripts/copy-node-runtime.mjs .next/standalone "$RUNNER_TEMP/stone-node-runtime"
      - name: Smoke the relocated runtime without credentials
        env:
          APP_ENV: production
          PLATFORM: node
          HOSTNAME: 127.0.0.1
          PORT: "3100"
          DATABASE_URL: ""
          BETTER_AUTH_SECRET: ""
          NODE_PATH: ""
        run: |
          runtime_pid=""
          cleanup() {
            if [ -n "$runtime_pid" ]; then
              kill "$runtime_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
              wait "$runtime_pid" 2>/dev/null || true
            fi
            cat "$RUNNER_TEMP/stone-node-runtime.log" || true
          }
          trap cleanup EXIT
          (cd "$RUNNER_TEMP/stone-node-runtime" && exec node server.js) > "$RUNNER_TEMP/stone-node-runtime.log" 2>&1 &
          runtime_pid=$!
          node scripts/smoke-packaged-app.mjs http://127.0.0.1:3100

  docker:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 25
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          # This job has no pnpm (the image installs its own); setup-node would otherwise try to
          # cache pnpm because package.json names it as the package manager.
          package-manager-cache: false
      - name: Build the Docker recipe without credentials
        run: docker build --progress=plain --build-arg INDEXING=off --tag stone:ci .
      - name: Smoke the non-root container without credentials
        run: |
          container_id=""
          cleanup() {
            if [ -n "$container_id" ]; then
              docker logs "$container_id" || true
              docker rm --force "$container_id" || true
            fi
          }
          trap cleanup EXIT
          container_id=$(docker run --detach --publish 127.0.0.1:3101:3000 stone:ci)
          test "$(docker exec "$container_id" id -u)" != "0"
          docker exec "$container_id" node --input-type=module -e 'import {assertInternalLinks} from "./copy-node-runtime.mjs"; assertInternalLinks(process.cwd());'
          node scripts/smoke-packaged-app.mjs http://127.0.0.1:3101

# ADR-001: Hosting and runtime

**Status:** Accepted (owner approved written ADR 2026-10-13)
**Date:** 2026-10-13

## Context

- STONE needs real authentication, server-side role checks and database access, so a pure static export is insufficient.
- The Cloudflare deployment is a **test environment** for building animations and features before handing the repository to other developers. It must be portable: a standard `next build` has to work on Node.js, Vercel or Netlify after only env/config changes.
- Budget: start on free tiers. Owner decision (2026-10-13, option A): stay on Workers Free; if the Worker exceeds the Free size limit, stop and ask before moving to Workers Paid.

Facts checked on 2026-10-13 (sources at the end):

- `@opennextjs/cloudflare` (latest 1.20.11) supports all Next.js 16 minors and the latest 14/15 minors, uses the Next.js Node.js runtime on Workers, supports standard middleware, and does **not** yet support Node middleware.
- OpenNext does not yet recognise the Next.js 16 `proxy.ts` file; `middleware.ts` still works in Next.js 16 (deprecated).
- Worker size limits: 3 MiB compressed (Free) and 10 MiB (Paid).
- OpenNext does not guarantee Windows builds; it recommends WSL, a Linux VM or Linux CI.
- Image optimisation on Cloudflare requires Cloudflare Images.
- Cloudflare's Next.js guide now recommends **vinext** (Vite-based reimplementation of the Next.js API, beta) as the default and keeps OpenNext for apps with compatibility gaps.
- Workers Builds connects a GitHub repository; production-branch pushes create deployments, other branches create Preview builds with Preview URLs that can be posted as PR comments.

## Decision

Run Next.js 16 on **Cloudflare Workers via `@opennextjs/cloudflare` 1.x**, deployed by **Workers Builds** connected to GitHub: `main` → stable test URL; every other branch/PR → Preview URL. Use the Workers Free plan.

All Cloudflare-specific code lives in `wrangler.jsonc`, `open-next.config.ts` and `src/server/platform/`. Application code uses only Next.js APIs and `process.env`.

## Options Considered

### Option A: OpenNext adapter on Workers (chosen)

| Dimension        | Assessment                                                     |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Complexity       | Medium: adapter config plus Linux-only Cloudflare build        |
| Cost             | Free plan; Paid ($5/month) only with owner approval if > 3 MiB |
| Scalability      | Sufficient for a test environment                              |
| Team familiarity | High: the app is plain Next.js; adapter is a build step        |

**Pros:** builds the real `next build` output, so other hosts run the same code; mature (1.x); per-branch previews; standard middleware supported.
**Cons:** no `proxy.ts` yet; 3 MiB Free limit is tight; Windows builds unsupported; image optimisation needs a workaround.

### Option B: vinext on Workers

| Dimension        | Assessment                                  |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Complexity       | Medium                                      |
| Cost             | Free plan                                   |
| Scalability      | Sufficient                                  |
| Team familiarity | Low: Vite-based reimplementation of Next.js |

**Pros:** Cloudflare's current default; Vite build; Cloudflare bindings.
**Cons:** beta; reimplements the Next.js surface, so the test environment would not run the same runtime as Vercel/Node targets; `next/*` imports "mostly supported", image optimisation partial. Conflicts with the portability goal.

### Option C: `@cloudflare/next-on-pages` (Pages)

**Pros:** simple Pages workflow. **Cons:** Edge runtime only; superseded by OpenNext. Rejected.

### Option D: Static export on Pages

**Pros:** cheapest and simplest. **Cons:** no server-side auth, server actions or role checks. Rejected.

### Option E: Vercel Hobby as the test host

**Pros:** zero-adapter Next.js. **Cons:** owner chose Cloudflare for testing; kept as the first migration target.

## Trade-off Analysis

Portability outweighs following Cloudflare's newest default. OpenNext adapts the genuine Next.js build output, so behaviour verified on the test environment transfers to other hosts. vinext may become preferable once stable, but adopting a beta reimplementation now would make the test environment diverge from the hand-off targets. The 3 MiB limit is the main operational risk; a CI size check makes it visible before deployment.

## Consequences

- Easier: per-PR preview URLs; leaving Cloudflare is a config change.
- Harder: Cloudflare builds only on Linux (Workers Builds and CI); local Windows development uses `next dev` only.
- Must use `middleware.ts`, not `proxy.ts`.
- Images: pre-optimised at build time for Cloudflare (static loader in the platform adapter); standard optimiser elsewhere.
- Every deployment is `noindex` (`X-Robots-Tag` + `robots.txt`) unless `INDEXING=on`.
- Revisit: `proxy.ts` support in OpenNext; vinext stability; Free size limit.

## Migration path

| Target           | Steps                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Vercel / Netlify | Import the repository; set env vars from `.env.example`; build command `pnpm build`. Delete `wrangler.jsonc` and `open-next.config.ts` (optional). Set `PLATFORM=node`.                                      |
| Node.js / Docker | `NEXT_OUTPUT=standalone pnpm build`; run with the provided Dockerfile (`node .next/standalone/server.js`); set env vars; put any Postgres URL in `DATABASE_URL` (the `pg` driver is selected automatically). |

Phase 5 performs and records a dry run of the Node/Docker path.

## Action Items

1. [ ] Phase 1: scaffold with `@opennextjs/cloudflare`, `wrangler.jsonc`, `open-next.config.ts`, `src/server/platform/`.
2. [ ] Phase 1: CI step that builds with OpenNext and fails above 3 MiB compressed.
3. [ ] Phase 1: owner connects Workers Builds (click-by-click steps in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`).
4. [ ] Phase 1: verify a PR preview URL in both locales.
5. [ ] Phase 5: non-Cloudflare dry run.

- https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/framework-guides/web-apps/nextjs/
- https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/ci-cd/builds/

# ADR-002: Authentication and database

**Status:** Accepted (owner approved written ADR 2026-10-13)
**Date:** 2026-10-13

## Context

- Roles: Guest (no session), Client (personal account), Admin (Client features plus the admin panel).
- Exactly two seeded test users (one Admin, one Client); credentials from git-ignored env only.
- Permission checks must be server-side (middleware plus a check in each server action and route handler).
- Criteria: portability across hosts, free tier, server-side role checks, simple seeding.
- The deployment is a test environment with no real personal data (owner, 2026-10-13). Production data residency (e.g. Russian 152-FZ) is out of scope and revisited before any production launch.

Facts checked on 2026-10-13:

- Auth.js (NextAuth) is now maintained by the Better Auth team, which recommends Better Auth for new projects.
- Better Auth supports PostgreSQL directly and via Drizzle/Prisma/Kysely adapters, provides a Next.js catch-all route handler, and on Workers needs `nodejs_compat` (AsyncLocalStorage).
- Supabase Free projects pause after 7 days of inactivity and need a manual restore; 2 active projects; 500 MB database.
- Neon Free: 100 CU-hours and 0.5 GB per project; compute suspends when idle and resumes on the next query.

## Decision

Use **Better Auth 1.x** (email + password, database sessions, admin/role support) with **PostgreSQL on Neon Free (EU region)** through **Drizzle ORM**.

The database driver is chosen in one file, `src/server/db/client.ts`, by the `DATABASE_URL`:

- Neon URL → `@neondatabase/serverless` HTTP driver (works on Workers and Node);
- any other `postgres://` URL → `pg`;
- `pglite://` → in-process PGlite for tests.

## Options Considered

### Option A: Better Auth + Neon Postgres + Drizzle (chosen)

| Dimension        | Assessment                                           |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Complexity       | Medium: auth tables and guards live in the repo      |
| Cost             | Free (Neon Free)                                     |
| Scalability      | Adequate; Postgres can move to any provider          |
| Team familiarity | High: TypeScript library, standard Postgres, Drizzle |

**Pros:** auth code is in the repository and works with any Postgres and any host; roles are a column checked by our own guards; seeding is a plain script; tests run against PGlite without network.
**Cons:** we own session/security configuration; no hosted dashboard for users; idle Neon compute adds a cold start.

### Option B: Supabase (Auth + Postgres + RLS)

| Dimension        | Assessment                                 |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Complexity       | Low–Medium: hosted auth, RLS policies      |
| Cost             | Free, but projects pause after 7 idle days |
| Scalability      | Good                                       |
| Team familiarity | Medium                                     |

**Pros:** auth, database and dashboard in one service; RLS as a second line of defence.
**Cons:** a test environment that is idle between work sessions and handed to other developers would regularly be paused; auth is tied to the Supabase service, so moving hosts is easy but moving away from Supabase is not.

### Option C: Auth.js + Postgres

**Pros:** large ecosystem. **Cons:** now in maintenance under Better Auth, which recommends Better Auth for new projects. Rejected.

### Option D: Hosted identity (Clerk, Auth0)

**Pros:** no auth code. **Cons:** vendor lock-in, account creation by the owner, client-heavy SDKs. Rejected for portability.

## Trade-off Analysis

Owning the auth layer costs some configuration effort but gives the strongest portability and the clearest server-side authorization model: one `role` column and explicit guards. Supabase's hosted convenience is outweighed by the 7-day pause on Free and by coupling auth to one vendor.

## Authorization model

| Layer                       | Responsibility                                                                                                                                              |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `middleware.ts`             | Optimistic cookie presence check for `/[locale]/account/*` and `/[locale]/admin/*`; redirect Guests to `/[locale]/sign-in?next=…`. Not a security boundary. |
| `src/server/auth/guards.ts` | `requireUser()`, `requireRole("admin")`: validate the session against the database. Called in every protected layout/page, server action and route handler. |
| CI test                     | Fails if an exported server action is not wrapped by a guard.                                                                                               |

Sign-up (Figma "Create account") always creates `role = "client"`. Admin exists only through the seed. Sign-out uses the Figma "Sign out" confirmation screen.

## Security baseline

- Cookies `httpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`; database-backed sessions and rate limiting.
- Secrets (`BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, `DATABASE_URL`, `SEED_*`) are server-only, validated by zod in `src/server/env.ts` with `import "server-only"`, never `NEXT_PUBLIC_`.
- `.env*` git-ignored; `.env.example` maintained.
- No email provider on the test environment: no verification or reset email (documented in `docs/SECURITY.md`).

## Data model (outline; exact schema approved in Phase 4)

- Better Auth: `user` (+ `role`), `session`, `account`, `verification`.
- App: `product`, `product_translation` (locale, name, description), `favorite`, `order`, `order_item`. Prices carry `is_placeholder` (USD 240/m² remains a placeholder).

## Consequences

- Easier: host migration; running tests offline; reasoning about permissions.
- Harder: we maintain auth configuration and upgrades.
- Phase 3 catalog uses a repository interface over static seed data; Phase 4 swaps it to Postgres.
- Revisit: production data residency and email delivery before any real launch.

## New dependencies

`better-auth`, `drizzle-orm`, `drizzle-kit` (dev), `@neondatabase/serverless`, `pg`, `@electric-sql/pglite` (dev/test), `zod`.

## Action Items

1. [ ] Phase 4 spec: schema, seed script, guard API, permission matrix (`docs/ROLES.md`).
2. [ ] Owner creates a Neon project (click-by-click steps in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`) and sets env vars in Cloudflare.
3. [ ] Access tests in CI: Guest redirected, Client denied admin, Admin allowed, in both locales.

- https://www.better-auth.com/docs/installation
- https://neon.com/pricing

# ADR-003: Styling system and design tokens

**Status:** Accepted (owner approved written ADR 2026-10-13)
**Date:** 2026-10-13

## Context

- Figma (`1vEGuD9cYYFNynyByUGHwF`) is the read-only source of truth. Its local variables already use CSS-like names (`--surface-page`, `--text-ink`, `--border-glass`, `--stone-catalog-card`, `--layout-margin`, `--type-*`), plus text styles (`Brand/Logo`, `Nav/Link`, `Catalog/Product name`, `Button/Label` …) and effect styles (`Surface/Glass panel`, `Blur/Glass background 24`).
- The palette, typefaces (Lusitana, Inter), imagery roles and D020 art direction are protected; deviations need explicit approval.
- Other developers will take over the codebase, so the styling layer should be widely known and hard to misuse.
- Lusitana (Google Fonts) has a **Latin subset only**; Inter covers Cyrillic. The Figma file is English, so Russian Lusitana-role text has no approved rendering.

Sample of variables read on 2026-10-13 (Home v2 — 1440, `722:1300`; Product / Black Marble — 1440, `782:11526`):

| Variable                                                                              | Value                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--surface-page`                                                                      | `#1b1d20`                                                             |
| `--surface-header`                                                                    | `#1214169e`                                                           |
| `--surface-panel`                                                                     | `#1214168c`                                                           |
| `--surface-button` / `--surface-nav-pill`                                             | `#ffffff14`                                                           |
| `--border-glass` / `--border-glass-strong`                                            | `#ffffff1f` / `#ffffff3d`                                             |
| `--text-primary` / `--text-secondary` / `--text-label`                                | `#ffffff` / `#ffffffb8` / `#ffffffcc`                                 |
| `--text-ink` / `--text-ink-secondary`                                                 | `#1b1c1e` / `#3a3d41`                                                 |
| `--stone-catalog-page` / `-card` / `-photo` / `-line` / `-ink` / `-secondary`         | `#f3f0eb` / `#f8f5f0` / `#e9e4dd` / `#d8d1c8` / `#292722` / `#625d55` |
| `--layout-margin` / `--layout-panel-pad` / `--layout-card-gap` / `--layout-control-h` | `77` / `24` / `24` / `40`                                             |

## Decision

Use **Tailwind CSS v4** on top of **CSS custom properties named exactly like the Figma variables**.

Pipeline:

1. Read variables with `get_variable_defs` (read-only) and store the snapshot in `src/styles/tokens/figma-variables.json`.
2. Generate/maintain `src/styles/tokens/*.css` (`color.css`, `type.css`, `layout.css`, `effects.css`, `motion.css`) with the same names and values.
3. Map them into Tailwind with `@theme inline` (e.g. `bg-surface-page`, `text-ink`, `border-glass`).
4. Reset Tailwind defaults (`--color-*: initial`, `--font-*: initial`) so non-STONE colours and fonts cannot be used.
5. `tokens.test.ts` fails if any Figma variable is missing or differs in CSS.

Typography: `next/font/google` (self-hosted at build time) for Inter and Lusitana. **Cyrillic glyphs in Lusitana roles fall back to PT Serif via `unicode-range`** (owner decision 2026-10-13, option A); Latin glyphs remain Lusitana. Final visual sign-off with ru/en screenshots side by side and a stone-art-direction review in Phase 2.

Figma letter-spacing values such as 14, 12, 10 are treated as percent and converted to `em` (0.14em …); verified with `get_design_context` in Phase 2.

## Options Considered

### Option A: Tailwind CSS v4 + CSS custom properties (chosen)

| Dimension        | Assessment                               |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Complexity       | Low: CSS-first config, no JS config file |
| Cost             | Build-time only, no runtime              |
| Scalability      | Good; tokens are plain CSS variables     |
| Team familiarity | High                                     |

**Pros:** familiar to most developers; tokens stay framework-agnostic CSS variables; default palette can be removed to protect the brand; good for state variants (`hover:`, `focus-visible:`, `disabled:`, `data-[state=…]`).
**Cons:** long class lists on complex glass components; needs a lint/format plugin for class ordering.

### Option B: CSS Modules + CSS custom properties

| Dimension        | Assessment        |
| ---------------- | ----------------- |
| Complexity       | Low               |
| Cost             | Zero dependencies |
| Scalability      | Good              |
| Team familiarity | High              |

**Pros:** no extra dependency; explicit per-component styles; same token layer.
**Cons:** more verbose; state variants and responsive rules written by hand; easier to drift from tokens (raw values in modules). A valid fallback.

### Option C: CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion)

**Cons:** runtime cost, friction with React Server Components. Rejected.

## Trade-off Analysis

Both A and B keep tokens in plain CSS variables, so the token layer is portable either way. Tailwind wins on hand-off familiarity and on making off-brand values impossible once defaults are reset. Complex glass effects are encapsulated in named utilities and components, so long class lists stay inside `src/components`.

## Consequences

- Easier: one source of token truth; brand drift caught by tests; new developers productive quickly.
- Harder: token snapshot must be refreshed manually (read-only) when Figma variables change.
- Approval required: the PT Serif Cyrillic fallback rendering (Phase 2); any new token not present in Figma.
- Revisit: if the owner supplies a licensed Cyrillic Lusitana-like face.

## New dependencies

`tailwindcss` v4, `@tailwindcss/postcss`, `prettier-plugin-tailwindcss` (dev).

1. [ ] Phase 1: Tailwind v4 setup with defaults reset.
2. [ ] Phase 2: full variable/style extraction for all frames in `docs/FIGMA-INVENTORY.md`; `tokens.test.ts`.
3. [ ] Phase 2: Cyrillic fallback sample on `/[locale]/_styleguide` for owner approval.

# ADR-004: Internationalisation and locale routing

**Status:** Accepted (owner approved written ADR 2026-10-13)
**Date:** 2026-10-13

## Context

- Locales: ru (default) and en. All user-facing strings live in `messages/ru.json` and `messages/en.json`; no hard-coded text.
- Public pages, auth pages, the account and the admin panel must work in both locales, including redirects behind auth.
- The language switch is a **button** (owner, 2026-10-13). Figma contains no language switcher, so it is built from the incumbent Nav/Pill component and approved visually in Phase 2.
- Must run on Workers (OpenNext, `middleware.ts`) and on Node/Vercel unchanged.

## Decision

Use **next-intl 4.x** with:

- `locales: ["ru", "en"]`, `defaultLocale: "ru"`, `localePrefix: "always"` (`/ru/…`, `/en/…`);
- `localeDetection: false` — `/` always redirects to `/ru`; a manual switch is remembered in the `NEXT_LOCALE` cookie;
- identical slugs in both locales (`/ru/catalog/black-marble`, `/en/catalog/black-marble`);
- a single `middleware.ts` composing next-intl first and the optimistic auth cookie check second; matcher excludes `/api`, `/_next` and static files;
- namespaced messages (`common`, `nav`, `footer`, `home`, `catalog`, `product`, `calculator`, `account`, `admin`, `auth`) typed through next-intl `AppConfig`;
- `react/jsx-no-literals` ESLint rule plus a key-parity test (identical keys, no empty values);
- product names and descriptions stored as data in `product_translation`, not in messages;
- numbers and prices through `format.number` (USD), units (m²) from messages; the placeholder price is labelled as illustrative;
- `<html lang>` per locale; `generateStaticParams` + `setRequestLocale` for static public pages.

## Options Considered

### Option A: next-intl (chosen)

| Dimension        | Assessment                             |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Complexity       | Low                                    |
| Cost             | Free, small runtime                    |
| Scalability      | Good                                   |
| Team familiarity | High; de facto standard for App Router |

**Pros:** Server Component support; typed keys; middleware for routing; ICU formatting.
**Cons:** middleware composition with auth must be written carefully.

### Option B: Hand-rolled dictionaries (Next.js docs pattern)

**Pros:** no dependency. **Cons:** no ICU plurals/formatting, typed keys and routing helpers must be built by hand. Rejected.

### Option C: i18next / react-i18next

**Pros:** large ecosystem. **Cons:** client-oriented, more setup for RSC. Rejected.

## Trade-off Analysis

next-intl gives typed keys, server rendering and routing with minimal code; its only cost is careful middleware composition, which is needed anyway for auth redirects. Always-prefixed URLs make locale explicit in every test and preview link.

## Consequences

- Easier: locale is visible in every URL; tests can target `/ru` and `/en` directly.
- Harder: Russian copy must be maintained for every new string (enforced by the parity test).
- Revisit: localised pathnames and `hreflang` when the site leaves `noindex`.

## New dependencies

# ADR-005: Testing and continuous integration

**Status:** Accepted (owner approved written ADR 2026-10-13)
**Date:** 2026-10-13

## Context

- Required test areas: access (roles), locale, order and form flows.
- Every PR must run lint, typecheck, unit tests, build and Playwright smoke, and must stay within the Cloudflare Workers Free size limit (ADR-001).
- Visual parity is checked at 1440, 1024, 768 and 390.

## Decision

- **Unit/integration:** Vitest + Testing Library (jsdom). Server code (guards, server actions, repositories) tested against **PGlite** (in-process Postgres) so CI needs no external database.
- **End-to-end:** Playwright in `tests/e2e/`: `access`, `locale`, `navigation`, `calculator`, `order`, `forms`, `smoke`. Accessibility with `@axe-core/playwright` on key pages.
- **Visual:** `tests/visual/` with Figma screenshots (via `get_screenshot`, read-only) committed as references at 1440/1024/768/390; threshold-based comparison, run only inside the official Playwright Linux container; comparison notes in `docs/QA/`.
- **CI:** GitHub Actions on every pull request:
  1. checkout, Node from `.nvmrc`, pnpm via corepack with cache;
  2. ESLint + Prettier check;
  3. `tsc --noEmit`;
  4. Vitest;
  5. `next build` (portability proof);
  6. OpenNext build + compressed size check (fail above 3 MiB);
  7. Playwright (Chromium desktop + mobile viewport) against `next start`.
     A separate manual workflow (`workflow_dispatch`, input: URL) runs smoke tests against a Cloudflare preview URL.
- Branch protection on `main` with required checks is enabled by the owner following steps in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`.

## Options Considered

### Option A: Vitest + Playwright + GitHub Actions (chosen)

| Dimension        | Assessment                    |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Complexity       | Low–Medium                    |
| Cost             | Free for a public repository  |
| Scalability      | Good; jobs can be split later |
| Team familiarity | High                          |

**Pros:** fast unit tests with native ESM/TS; Playwright covers e2e, a11y and screenshots in one tool; PGlite removes external DB from CI.
**Cons:** visual baselines are OS-sensitive (mitigated by the Linux container).

### Option B: Jest + Cypress

**Pros:** familiar. **Cons:** slower, heavier ESM/TS setup; Cypress weaker for multi-viewport screenshots. Rejected.

### Option C: Chromatic/Percy for visual testing

**Pros:** hosted visual review. **Cons:** external account and paid tiers. Rejected for now.

## Trade-off Analysis

Vitest and Playwright are the current defaults for Next.js and need no paid services. Comparing against Figma screenshots cannot be pixel-exact because browser and Figma font rendering differ, so thresholds plus written QA notes are used instead of a hard pixel gate.

## Consequences

- Easier: every PR proves build portability and size budget; access rules are regression-tested.
- Harder: visual references must be refreshed (read-only) when Figma changes.
- Revisit: a second e2e run against real Postgres once Phase 4 lands.

## Request flow

1. `src/middleware.ts` first applies the route gate (`src/lib/route-gate.ts`, below), then next-intl maps `/` → `/ru`, keeps `/ru/*` and `/en/*`, and redirects paths without a locale to `/ru/<path>`. Before that, an optimistic auth check sends a Guest without a session cookie from `/{locale}/account/*` and `/{locale}/admin/*` to `/{locale}/sign-in?next=…` (`next` sanitised by `src/lib/safe-next.ts`), and every request gets the `x-stone-path` header for the guards. The cookie is not proof: `requireUser` / `requireRole` in `src/server/auth/guards.ts` validate the session against the database (Better Auth, cookie cache off) in every protected page, action and route.
2. `src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx` validates the locale (`hasLocale` → `notFound()`; `dynamicParams = false` is not used, it broke `/ru` and `/en` on Workers), renders `<html lang>` and provides messages.
3. `next.config.ts` inlines `INDEXING` at build time and adds `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow` to every response unless it is `on`; `src/app/robots.ts` reads the same inlined value. `public/_headers` adds the header to static files that bypass Next.js on Cloudflare/Netlify.
4. Unknown paths under a locale are rewritten by the route gate to `src/app/[locale]/(site)/404/page.tsx` with status 404. `[...rest]` (`notFound()`) remains as the fallback for paths the middleware matcher skips.
5. On Cloudflare, pages are rendered per request (OpenNext default, no incremental cache). The read-only static-assets cache was tried and returned 404 for prerendered pages (`NoFallbackError`); revisit with an R2/KV cache when traffic or CPU limits require it.

## Route gate and the localised 404

Decision (Phase 3 final review, I1 and I2): `src/middleware.ts` runs `gateRoute()` from `src/lib/route-gate.ts` before next-intl.

- The gate no longer knows which products exist. Since Phase 4a the catalog is in the database and the middleware cannot await a database on every host (Edge runtime, Workers), so it only normalises and checks shape. A product slug (`catalog/<slug>`, `admin/products/<slug>`) that is lowercase and shaped like a slug (`SLUG_SHAPE`: letters, digits, single dashes) passes. The same slug in another case or encoding (`/ru/catalog/Black-Marble`) gets a 308 to the lowercase form. A segment that is not a slug (dots, spaces, double dashes, bad escapes) and any other path under a locale that is not in `PUBLIC_ROUTES` is rewritten to `/{locale}/404` with status 404. The browser keeps the requested URL.
- Why not `dynamicParams = false` on `catalog/[slug]`: that is the standard fix, but it is the same switch that broke `/ru` and `/en` on Workers at the locale level (OpenNext has no incremental cache here, the prerender lookup fails, `NoFallbackError`), and it would make a product created in the admin a 404 until the next build.
- Why the product page is rendered per request (`export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"`, Phase 4a Task 5): an unknown slug of the right shape reaches the route, which would call `notFound()`. On an SSG route with on-demand ISR Next stores that 404 in the route cache like any page. Measured with `next start`: the first request to `/ru/catalog/nope` answered 404 and the next one `x-nextjs-cache: HIT` with `Cache-Control: s-maxage=31536000`: one cache entry (and one CDN entry) per requested slug, without bound, and a stale 404 for a slug that is created later unless every creation revalidates it. There is no per-slug opt-out: calling a dynamic API (`connection()`) in the not-found branch makes the on-demand render answer 500. Per-request rendering answers "200" or "404, `no-store`", shows an admin's edit, unpublish or new product at once, and does not depend on `revalidatePath` (Cloudflare has no incremental cache and renders per request anyway). Historically, Home stayed static and needed concrete `/ru` and `/en` invalidation; Phase 4b Site content now renders Home per request too. Admin actions retain concrete Home/catalog paths and account/admin invalidation for client navigation. Cost: two small queries per product page view. `tests/e2e/not-found.spec.ts` and `tests/e2e/admin.spec.ts` hold the behaviour: `Black-Marble` and `nope` requested, then `black-marble` is still 200, and a product created under the slug that was a 404 is 200 at once.
- Why a page and not `notFound()`: `notFound()` thrown during render escapes the HTML shell (React's server renderer has no error boundaries). Next then sends the empty `<html id="__next_error__">` recovery shell with status 404, and the not-found UI appears only after client-side rendering. Without JavaScript the page was blank, and this predates Phase 3. `(site)/404/page.tsx` is a normal, dynamic render, so the h1, body and catalog link are in the server HTML. Next takes the metadata of any 404-status response from the nearest `not-found.tsx`, so the localised `<title>` (`meta.notFound`) is exported there.
- Maintenance: a new page under `src/app/[locale]` must be added to `PUBLIC_ROUTES`, or it will be served as a 404. `tests/unit/route-gate.test.ts` scans the app directory and fails when a page is missing.
- Unknown or unpublished product slug (Phase 4a Task 5, fix round 1): `catalog/[slug]` does `redirect(`/${locale}/404`)` (307, `no-store`), and the gate's server-rendered 404 page answers 404 with `lang`, the localised h1, title and `noindex`. Why not `notFound()`: in Next 16.3.8 the not-found boundary is a client component and React's server renderer never runs error boundaries, so `notFound()` thrown during render ends in the empty `__next_error__` shell (measured at 39084a0: 404, no `lang`, no h1, content only after client rendering). The redirect keeps the content in the server HTML, nothing is cached (the route is `force-dynamic`), and a product that exists costs nothing extra. Cost, for the owner checklist: the address bar shows `/ru/404` for an unknown product, and the answer is 307 then 404 instead of one 404. A Suspense wrapper was rejected (a streamed 200 soft 404), and so was a database check in the middleware (Edge runtime: `pg` and PGlite cannot load there). `tests/e2e/not-found.spec.ts` covers 307 then 404, the localised page with JavaScript disabled, and that nothing is cached. Admin pages (`admin/products/[slug]`) still use `notFound()`: the admin area needs JavaScript anyway.
- Other limits: single-segment dotted paths (`/zz.txt`) reach the `[locale]` route outside the middleware matcher, which predates Phase 3.

## Portability rules

- Application code imports `@/server/platform`, never `@opennextjs/cloudflare`, `wrangler` or `cloudflare:*` (ESLint rule + `tests/unit/structure.test.ts`).
- Environment is read via `process.env` and validated in `src/server/env.ts`.
- Next.js is pinned to `16.3.8`: Next 16.4.0 crashes on Workers with `Unexpected loadManifest(/.next/server/preview-props.json)` until OpenNext ships the fix (opennextjs/opennextjs-cloudflare#1448, PR #1356). The `cloudflare` CI job smoke-tests the built Worker in workerd, so an upgrade that breaks the runtime fails CI.
- `cacheComponents` is off until OpenNext supports it on Workers (see ADR-001 and the Phase 1 plan ledger notes in the PR).

## Layout notes for Phase 3

- `TabBar` is `position: fixed` at the bottom of the viewport on phones: visible below 768 px (`md:hidden`), 358 x 68, 16 px above the bottom edge or the safe-area inset, whichever is larger.
- Pages and layouts that render it need 100 px of bottom padding (bar 68 + bottom offset `max(16px, env(safe-area-inset-bottom))` + 16 px breathing room). Use the `pb-tabbar` utility from `src/app/globals.css`, phones only: `max-md:pb-tabbar`.
- The `[locale]` layout mounts both `TabBar` and `SiteFooter` in Phase 3 (neither is mounted anywhere yet). The footer is full width; the bar floats above it.
- `TabBar`'s `current` prop is optional: product pages (`/catalog/<slug>`) highlight Catalog, as Figma's Product screen (782:11815) draws it active.
- Shell mounting (Task 4): `src/app/[locale]/(site)/layout.tsx` renders `SiteHeader`, the single `<main>` (pages never render their own), `SiteFooter` and `ShellTabBar` (client; maps the locale-stripped `usePathname()` to `TabBarCurrent`), with the phone padding on the footer, 24 px own + 100 px bar space (`<SiteFooter reserveTabBar>` -> `max-md:pb-footer-tabbar`), not on the wrapper, so the footer glass extends under the floating bar. `[locale]/layout.tsx` keeps `<html>`, `<body>` and providers only. `/_styleguide` is outside the `(site)` group, so it has no shell. `(site)/not-found.tsx` renders the localised 404 inside the shell; `[locale]/not-found.tsx` is the fallback.
- Controls whose pages do not exist yet are inert (non-link `span`, `aria-disabled`), listed in `INERT` (`src/components/navigation/nav-items.ts`, called `PHASE3_INERT` in Phase 3): header and menu Create Your Stone and Cart; tab bar Cart. Favorites and the account entries went live in Phase 4a. Remove an entry when its page ships.
- The account entries are session-aware (Phase 4a): the header account button, the mobile menu entry and the last tab ("Sign in" for a Guest, "Account" once signed in) go to `/sign-in` for a Guest and `/account` otherwise. The public pages are static, so the visitor state is a client island: `AccountStateProvider` (`src/features/account`, mounted in the `(site)` layout) fetches `GET /api/me` after hydration (no-store; signed-in flag, display name, favourite slugs; never an id or email) and re-reads it after each navigation. The ♥ of the catalog and showcase cards and the product page Save read it and toggle through the guarded `toggleFavorite` server action (optimistic, the wanted state is sent so a stale client cannot flip the wrong way); a Guest is sent to `/sign-in?next=<page and query>` and the click is added once they are back (sessionStorage, 30 minutes). Trade-off: a signed-in visitor sees an unsaved heart for the moment between hydration and the answer; the alternative, reading the session in the layout, would make every public page dynamic. `html[data-account-state]` (loading, guest, signed-in) is the readiness signal for tests.

### Guards

- One boundary: `requireUser(locale)` / `requireRole("admin", locale)`. They read the session from the database on every call (`getSession` is wrapped in React `cache`, so the second call in a request is free). A Guest is redirected to `/{locale}/sign-in?next=<page>`; a signed-in user without the role gets `notFound()`.
- Called in the layout, in **every** page and as the **first statement** of every server action; a layout is not re-rendered on every client navigation, so the layout call alone is not a boundary. The middleware only does an optimistic cookie check.
- The page path reaches the guards through the `x-stone-path` request header, which the middleware always overwrites; actions get the locale from it (`requestLocale()`).
- Enforced by `tests/unit/server-actions-guarded.test.ts` (static scan of every `"use server"` module and route handler) and `tests/e2e/access.spec.ts`.
- Better Auth is used through its handler (`callAuthEndpoint`), never `auth.api.*`, because only the handler applies rate limiting and the origin check. Results given to the browser go through `toClientResult` (no session token).

`getDb()` is async and returns `null` without `DATABASE_URL`. The route gate (`src/lib/route-gate.ts`) normalises and checks the **shape** of a product slug (lowercase `a-z0-9` with single dashes; another case or encoding gets a 308 to the lowercase form; anything else is a 404). ### Worker bundle guard

Turbopack writes the shared server chunks once per route group, so Better Auth, Drizzle and zod were bundled once for the public pages, once for the account pages and once for the auth pages (about 330 KiB gzip of copies; the Worker limit is 3 MiB). Two measures keep it at one copy:

1. `src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx` imports `@/server/auth/guards` and `@/server/account/queries` for their side effects (they only declare functions). The common parent puts those modules into one shared chunk. **Do not remove those imports**, and add a module there when a new route group pulls in a big server dependency (the admin group reused the shared copy without a change).
2. `pnpm cf:size` (`scripts/check-worker-size.mjs`, pure parts in `scripts/worker-size.mjs`, unit-tested) prints the ten largest server chunks and **fails when the Better Auth marker is in more than one `chunks/ssr` file**, or in none (a stale marker). It runs in the CI `cloudflare` job after `pnpm cf:build`.

# Portable Node and Docker package

This packages the demo for customer approval and source handover to another team.
It does not provision the receiving team's host or perform a hosting migration.
Cloudflare/OpenNext remains the test target. The normal `pnpm build` is unchanged;
only `pnpm build:node` selects Next's `output: "standalone"`.

## Build and run

Use Node 24 and the pinned pnpm with the frozen lockfile. Build from a clean source
copy containing the intended commit **and any approved uncommitted changes**.
Do not copy `.env*` (except examples), `.data`, `.git`, caches or internal work reports.
Prefer a fresh checkout, or place a source export outside any ancestor repository's
ignored directory. Tailwind source scanning can inherit parent ignore rules; the
Phase 5 export test required its own disposable Git boundary for this reason.
`build:node` refuses local environment files because Next can copy them into the
standalone artifact. It also clears known inherited database/auth/seed values for
the build child. Secrets belong in the runtime process, never build args.

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm build:node
```

`scripts/build-node.mjs` builds Next and copies `public`, `.next/static` and
`drizzle` into `.next/standalone`. The generated `server.js` and traced dependencies
are the runtime. Generated dependency links are verified to target traced packages
inside the artifact. Windows junctions use absolute paths, so use the supplied
copier to rebase them when moving to a new runtime directory:

```sh
node scripts/copy-node-runtime.mjs .next/standalone ../stone-runtime
```

The copier refuses an existing destination or an external dependency link. It is
also included as `copy-node-runtime.mjs` in the artifact for later relocation.
Do not drag-copy a Windows junction tree and assume it is independent. Build and
run on compatible OS/architecture; Windows artifacts
are not Linux container artifacts. No full repository, pnpm, migration CLI, seed
script or dev server is required to serve the package.

Start from the runtime directory with `node server.js`, injecting these variables:

| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `HOSTNAME=127.0.0.1`, `PORT=3100`     | Local smoke binding; use `0.0.0.0` only inside an isolated container/private host as appropriate. |
| `PLATFORM=node`, `APP_ENV=production` | Real Node deployment; production hides styleguide and enforces secure cookies.                    |
| `DATABASE_URL`, `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`  | Runtime database and a unique secret; absent database gives the public no-auth mode.              |

## Editor and storefront

The product editor accepts JPEG/JFIF, PNG, WebP, AVIF, BMP and HEIC/HEIF originals
up to 30 MiB and 60,000,000 pixels each. Files are identified by their contents;
missing or incorrect browser MIME types do not reject a valid photo. A product
has up to eight ordered images; the first image is its card/main image. Admins can
select multiple files, make an image main, move it earlier/later, remove it from
the gallery, and add an existing catalog asset. To replace an image, add the new
one and remove the old one. At least one image is required when saving.

Uploads complete before Save draft / Publish / Save changes become available.
An upload does not publish the product. Completed uploads remain in the editor if
a later file fails. A failed save preserves the fields and selected images.

The browser checks header dimensions before decoding, applies image orientation,
strips metadata and normalizes to PNG,
with a maximum side of 1600 pixels and a maximum encoded size of 2 MiB. It tries
smaller sizes down to 800 pixels when necessary. The server independently checks
the signature, dimensions, bounded inflation, PNG chunks, CRC and decoded bytes,
then re-encodes the image. Each photo is prepared in a fresh dedicated browser
worker and the files are processed sequentially. The worker (and any nested HEIC
decoder) is terminated on completion, error or the two-minute preparation timeout.
HEIC/HEIF uses native decoding when available, otherwise a lazy-loaded `heic-to`
1.6.6 decoder; photos are never sent to an external conversion service. The decoder
is a client worker asset, not a server dependency. See `THIRD_PARTY.md` for notices.
The editor distinguishes preparation, uploading, byte/pixel limit errors and
unreadable files, preserves completed uploads, and enables retry after failure.
SVG, animated formats and arbitrary external URLs are
not accepted. The existing private request-photo limits remain unchanged.

Published cards use the main image. The product page switches between real photos
without cropping them. Existing single-asset products retain their full/detail
view. No unrelated mobile styles or navigation were changed.

# Security

Reference for the auth, session, database and admin setup (Phase 4a, ADR-002). Who may do what is in `docs/ROLES.md`; the owner steps to configure a deployment are in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`. Status: reviewed by an independent security review after Task 2 (auth core) and during Tasks 3 to 5, and audited as a whole at the end of Phase 4a (findings F1 to F11, handled below); Phase 4b gets its own review.

This is a **test environment with fake data and no real personal data** (ADR-002). The controls below are real nonetheless, because the code is meant to carry over to production. Production data residency (for example 152-FZ), a privacy notice and email verification are out of scope here and must be decided before a real launch.

Sign-up does reveal a taken email (accepted, below)                                                                |

## Authorization

- `src/middleware.ts` only checks that a session cookie is present for `/{locale}/account/*` and `/{locale}/admin/*`. It is not a security boundary.
- `requireUser()` and `requireRole("admin")` in `src/server/auth/guards.ts` validate the session against the database (the cookie cache is off, and `getSession` also passes `disableCookieCache`). Every protected layout, page, server action and route handler calls one of them, as the **first statement** of an action. A non-admin gets a 404 for admin pages (`docs/ROLES.md` explains the choice).
- Sign-up always creates a `client`. `role` cannot be set through sign-up or update-user (and there is no public route to either). An Admin exists only through `pnpm db:seed`.
- `next` redirect targets go through `sanitizeNext()`: only internal paths of the current locale are accepted; `//evil.com`, `https:evil.com`, `/\evil.com`, `%2F%2Fevil.com`, control characters, the sign-in and sign-up pages (a loop) and `/sign-out` are refused.
- The raw request headers carry whatever the client sent. The internal `x-stone-client-ip` header is ours alone: `callAuthEndpoint` and `getSession` delete a client-supplied value.

## Server actions and route handlers

- A server action is a public `POST` endpoint. Each one guards first, then validates its `unknown` arguments with zod, then acts on the session's user (account) or on admin data (admin).
- Call Better Auth through `callAuthEndpoint()` (`src/server/auth/next.ts`), not `auth.api.*`. It calls the Better Auth handler in-process, and only the handler applies rate limiting and the origin check. **There is no HTTP route to Better Auth** (`/api/auth/*` answers 404, F1): the browser never needs one, and a public catch-all would expose every endpoint Better Auth has now or gains in an upgrade (`get-session`, `list-sessions`, `update-user`, ...). `AuthEndpoint` lists the four endpoints the actions use.
- Names and images: the app validates names itself (length 1 to 80, trimmed, no control or invisible formatting characters, `src/lib/plain-text.ts`). A `hooks.before` in `src/server/auth/auth.ts` applies the same rule to Better Auth's own `sign-up/email` and `update-user` input and rejects any `image` (F2), so a future route or script cannot bypass it. Product names and descriptions in the admin actions follow the same rule (a description may also have line feeds).
- Sign-in and sign-up results contain the raw session token. Return only `toClientResult(result)` (a code and a status, never data) to the browser. Server actions return codes and the saved value only (`src/features/account/results.ts`, `src/features/admin/results.ts`).
- `GET /api/me` and `GET /api/health/db` are public by design (`docs/ROLES.md`). Both are `no-store`. `/api/health/db` runs `select 1` per hit: do not point a short-interval uptime monitor at it (it keeps a free Neon database awake and spends compute hours).

## CSRF and origin checks

- **Server actions:** Next.js compares the `Origin` header with the host of the request and rejects a mismatch. Session cookies are `SameSite=Lax`, so a cross-site `POST` does not carry them anyway. There is no `allowedOrigins` setting; the app is served from one host. If a deployment sits behind a proxy that rewrites the `Host` header, forward `X-Forwarded-Host` so the two agree.
- **Better Auth calls** (the in-process calls of our actions; there is no HTTP route): the origin check is on (`disableOriginCheck: false`, `disableCSRFCheck: false`; Better Auth would switch it off under `NODE_ENV=test`, so it is set explicitly). Trusted origins are the origins of `BETTER_AUTH_URL` and `SITE_URL`. A `POST` with a foreign or missing `Origin` is refused (403, tested).
- **Sign-out** is a `POST` server action; a `GET` (or a link prefetch) only renders the confirmation question.
- The base URL used for the internal request to Better Auth is the configured one, otherwise the request host over https (plain http only for `localhost`); `X-Forwarded-Proto` is ignored on purpose.

## Cookies and sessions

- Sign-out redirects home only after the handler succeeds. A rejected or unavailable request retains the cookie and shows a localized retry message, also without JavaScript. A failed session lookup on the confirmation page is treated as unknown, not as a Guest.
- Better Auth 1.7.7's sign-out endpoint catches revocation errors; its `deleteWithHooks` can also swallow a preliminary read failure. Our before-hook therefore confirms a parameterized Drizzle DELETE of the caller's signed session token before the endpoint can clear the cookie. Rate limiting and origin validation still run first. This applies to the current database-only, credentials-only configuration; revisit it before adding secondary session storage, provider logout or session deletion hooks.

- The session cookie is `stone.session_token` (`__Secure-stone.session_token` over https): `httpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Path=/`, `Secure`. The only exception is a base URL of plain-http `localhost`.
- If neither `BETTER_AUTH_URL` nor `SITE_URL` is set, cookies are Secure unless `APP_ENV=development`, the default. **A Node host must therefore set `APP_ENV=production` (or an https `BETTER_AUTH_URL`).** Otherwise its cookies are not Secure.
- Sessions live 7 days and are refreshed at most once a day. They are database rows: signing out deletes the row and clears the cookie; changing the password ends every other session of the user and **rotates this one** (a new token and cookie, so a token that leaked before the change is dead, F6). A changed role or a revoked session applies on the next request, because nothing is cached.

### Auth error diagnostics

`src/server/auth/diagnostics.ts` emits fixed event categories and allowlisted error names / driver codes only. It discards messages, stacks, SQL parameters, arbitrary names/codes and other arguments, including nested driver payloads. The Better Auth custom logger and API-error callback both use it. The callback converts non-API errors into a generic APIError so Better Call's fallback cannot print the original error. `callAuthEndpoint` also catches failures outside that router boundary. Unknown categories remain observable as `auth_error` / `unknown`; no raw payload is required for diagnosis.

## Rate limiting

- Better Auth stores rate limits in the `rate_limit` table, keyed by client IP and path, so the limit holds across Worker isolates and Node processes. The limits are sign-in 10/min, sign-up 5/min, change-password 5/min and everything else 100/min (`RATE_LIMIT_RULES` in `src/server/auth/auth.ts`). Counted on every attempt, successful or not.
- The client IP comes from the platform adapter (`clientIp` in `src/server/platform`). The auth entry points copy it into an internal header and overwrite any value the client sent.

| Host                                                                                 | IP source                          | Condition and caveat                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Cloudflare Workers** (the test environment)                                        | `cf-connecting-ip`                 | Cloudflare sets it at the edge and overwrites a client value. There is no other way to reach the Worker, so it cannot be forged.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Node behind one proxy** (Vercel, Netlify, nginx with `$proxy_add_x_forwarded_for`) | the **last** `X-Forwarded-For` hop | The proxy must overwrite or append to `X-Forwarded-For`; the last hop is the address the proxy saw. If clients can reach `next start` directly, they choose the value and can evade the limit.                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **A Node origin behind Cloudflare** (`CF -> Node`)                                   | last `X-Forwarded-For` hop         | Cloudflare appends the client address, so the last hop is the client. **The origin must accept connections only from Cloudflare's IP ranges** (firewall or Authenticated Origin Pulls); otherwise anyone can talk to it directly and choose the header.                                                                                                                                                  |
| **`CF -> nginx -> Node`**                                                            | last `X-Forwarded-For` hop         | nginx appends the address it saw, which is the Cloudflare **edge** IP. Every visitor behind that edge shares one bucket: legitimate users lock each other out after 10 sign-in attempts a minute. Fix on nginx: restore the real address with the `real_ip` module (`set_real_ip_from <Cloudflare ranges>; real_ip_header CF-Connecting-IP;`) and pass `proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;`. |
| **Hops with a port** (`203.0.113.7:51234`, as some Azure services send)              | last hop, **not validated**        | Better Auth's IP check refuses the value and the request falls into the shared "no IP" bucket (and the one-time warning does not fire). Strip the port at the proxy.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

- Without any client IP, all requests share one bucket per path and a warning is logged once ("rate limiting falls back to one shared bucket"). That is safe (stricter), but one visitor can lock the others out.
- The e2e server runs behind no proxy; `tests/e2e/auth-fixtures.ts` gives every test its own `X-Forwarded-For` so tests never share a bucket.

## Passwords

- Hashing is Better Auth's default, **scrypt**, with its own salt per user; verification is constant-time. Minimum 8 and maximum 128 characters (the maximum bounds the hashing cost an attacker can request).
- **Workers Free CPU risk.** Workers Free allows about 10 ms of CPU per request. A scrypt hash with Better Auth's parameters takes tens of milliseconds on a normal server CPU, so sign-in and sign-up **may fail on the Cloudflare preview** with a CPU-limit error (Worker exceeded CPU time limit, Cloudflare error 1102). It cannot be tested locally, only on the preview once Neon is configured (`docs/DEPLOYMENT.md`, section "Check the preview"). If it fails, the options are: (a) a Workers Paid plan (rejected by the owner so far: no paid plan); (b) replace the hash with WebCrypto **PBKDF2** through Better Auth's `emailAndPassword.password.hash` / `verify` override (native code, far cheaper than scrypt written in JavaScript; the iteration count must be measured on the preview, because a count that is strong enough may still be tight inside 10 ms); (c) host the test environment on a Node platform. **Choosing (b) is the owner's decision**: it changes how passwords are stored, so existing seed users must be recreated after the switch. Do not change the algorithm without that decision.

## Accounts and email

- Errors for an unknown email and a wrong password are identical (`INVALID_EMAIL_OR_PASSWORD`, 401).
- There is **no email service** on the test environment. Consequences: no email verification (an address is not proven to belong to the person who typed it), no password reset ("I forgot my password" has no answer; an Admin would have to reseed or edit the database), no email change, no notifications. A real launch needs an email provider (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) before any of these is turned on.
- Better Auth logs at the error level only, because lower levels log email addresses (a duplicate sign-up is logged at info). Telemetry is off.

## Database and seed

- All database code is in `src/server/db`. Queries are built with Drizzle (parameterised); there is no string-built SQL with user input.
- Migrations are committed (`drizzle/`) and applied with `pnpm db:migrate`. The Neon driver is the HTTP one (no persistent connection); admin writes use one atomic unit (`db.batch` on Neon, a transaction elsewhere).
- Seed rules (`pnpm db:seed`, `src/server/db/seed.ts`):
  - the Admin and the Client are created through Better Auth's hashing; emails are lowercased; passwords come from `SEED_*` and are never printed (the seed prints counts only);
  - it only inserts missing rows and never overwrites products, translations or orders an admin has edited;
  - an existing account is promoted to Admin only if it already holds `SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD`; otherwise the seed throws `SeedRefusalError` (names variables, never values) and stops. If `SEED_ADMIN_EMAIL` was pre-registered by someone else, the seed refuses rather than hand them the role;
  - it refuses a remote database (anything but `pglite://` or a postgres URL on `localhost`) unless `SEED_ALLOW_REMOTE=1` is set, and then only with a `SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD` of at least 16 characters (the refusal names the variable, never the value; F4);
  - the demo orders and favourites attach to the account that holds `SEED_CLIENT_EMAIL`; if someone pre-registered that address, the (fake) demo data attaches to their account (low).
- Use strong, unique passwords for the **preview** seed users: the preview is reachable by anyone who has the URL, and the Admin account can edit the catalog.
- Tests and CI use a throwaway PGlite database and the obviously fake values of `.env.test.example`. They never touch Neon.

## Response headers

Every response carries (`src/server/security-headers.ts`, applied by `next.config.ts`; the same lines are in `public/_headers` for the static files that bypass Next, and `tests/unit/next-config.test.ts` keeps them equal; `poweredByHeader` is off):

| Header                    | Value                                                                            |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'; object-src 'none'` |
| `X-Content-Type-Options`  | `nosniff`                                                                        |
| `Referrer-Policy`         | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`                                                |
| `Permissions-Policy`      | `camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()`                                       |
| `X-Robots-Tag`            | `noindex, nofollow` unless `INDEXING=on`                                         |

**No `script-src` yet, on purpose.** Next's own inline bootstrap scripts need a per-request nonce, which means a middleware nonce and dynamic rendering of every page. Home now renders per request for content freshness, but that does not implement nonce infrastructure or a script policy. A Report-Only script policy is also deferred: it would only produce noise until the nonce exists. HSTS is left to the host (Cloudflare and Vercel send it on their own domains; set it on the custom domain at launch).

## Accepted for the test deployment

These are known and accepted while the site holds fake data and the audience is the owner and testers.

1. **Sign-up reveals a taken email** ("this address is already registered"). Accepted in the spec; the sign-in screen does not reveal anything. Mitigated by the 5/min sign-up limit per IP.
2. **`GET /api/me` is public.** By design. It answers only for the caller's own session and returns no id or email.
3. **`GET /api/health/db` is public** and wakes a suspended Neon database.
4. **No email verification, no password reset** (no email service).
5. **F5 (resolved by F1).** Better Auth's own HTTP surface is not exposed, so its per-endpoint behaviour (session listing, `update-user`, ...) is not reachable and needs no separate review until a route is added.
6. **F4, partly handled.** The remote seed needs an admin password of at least 16 characters. Still open: the sign-in limit is per IP and path, **not per email**, so a distributed attack on one admin address is not slowed down; the admin has **no second factor**; a session lives **7 days**. Acceptable with fake data; see "Before production".
7. **F7: previews and production share one Neon project and secret** until real data exists. Anyone with a preview address (every pull-request branch has one) talks to the same database and the same `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`. Fine for fake data. **Before any real data:** a separate Neon branch (own `DATABASE_URL`) and a separate `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` for previews, so a preview can never read or sign for production.
8. **F8: no edge rate limit.** The auth rate limit lives in the database and counts only sign-in, sign-up and change-password. Server actions in general (favourites, admin writes) and `/api/*` have none, and a burst spends Worker and Neon quota. **Before production:** a Cloudflare rate-limiting rule for `POST` requests that carry a `Next-Action` header and for `/api/*` (Security, WAF, Rate limiting rules; verify in the current dashboard), for example 60 requests a minute per IP, plus a lower limit on the sign-in and sign-up pages.
9. **Workers Free CPU limit vs scrypt** (see "Passwords"): open until checked on the preview; the fix is an owner decision.
10. **A signed-in visitor sees an unsaved heart for a moment** on a full page load of a static page, until `/api/me` answers. Cosmetic.
11. **The 404 for unknown products is a 307 to `/{locale}/404`** (Next 16.3.8 cannot render a server-side 404 from a `notFound()` thrown during render); the URL changes. Not a security issue, listed because the owner decides on it.
12. **Rate limiting depends on how the host supplies the client IP** (table above). A host that does not meet its row weakens or over-tightens the limit.
13. **The Neon batch write path is tested only against a fake handle** here; it runs for real for the first time on the preview.
14. **Neon Free compute hours.** Each public page view runs 2 to 6 queries, so steady traffic keeps the database awake all month: about 182 compute hours against the 100 free ones. With real traffic the free plan runs out; budget for the paid plan or reduce queries (one cached catalog load per request) before launch. When the cap is hit the database stops answering and the site returns errors (the localised error page) until the month ends.
15. **Cloudflare Workers Free has request and CPU quotas**: a burst of traffic can make the preview return errors. It is a test environment.
16. **No `script-src` in the CSP** (see "Response headers").

## Before production

In this order of importance:

1. **Real data separation (F7):** a separate Neon branch and `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` for previews; production secrets never set on preview deployments.
2. **Brute-force and abuse limits (F4, F8):** a per-email sign-in limit (counted by normalised email, in addition to the per-IP one), the Cloudflare rate-limiting rule for `Next-Action` POSTs and `/api/*`, and an alert on repeated sign-in failures for the admin address.
3. **Admin hardening (F4):** a second factor for the Admin (Better Auth two-factor plugin or the identity provider of the company), a shorter admin session (for example 8 hours with re-authentication for destructive actions), and a way to list and revoke sessions.
4. **Email:** a provider (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), email verification and password reset.
5. **Password hash:** the decision on scrypt vs PBKDF2 vs Argon2 on a paid plan (see "Passwords").
6. **Headers:** a nonce-based `script-src` (and `style-src`), first as Report-Only, then enforced; HSTS on the real domain.
7. **Launch switches:** `INDEXING=on` and the removal of the noindex rule in `public/_headers`; `APP_ENV=production`; a real domain in `BETTER_AUTH_URL`.
8. **Compliance:** data residency and a privacy notice (for example 152-FZ), and a second security review of 4b.

## Local Phase 4b content and concurrency follow-up

Product updates, publish changes and Promotions now require the revision loaded with their form. A conditional write increments it; a stale form receives a conflict and retains its input. Full product fields and both translations commit in one SQL statement, so a failed translation cannot leave a partial product update. Revision overflow is refused. Initial seeding and repair scripts remain maintenance operations; they must not run concurrently with editors.

Site content actions authorize before parsing input, allow only the 18 existing home text keys and `ru`/`en`, and compare the stored text before replacing or restoring an override. Independent fields do not conflict; a text value changed away and back is intentionally treated as the same baseline. Overrides render as escaped text, without HTML or ICU evaluation. Missing overrides and an unconfigured database use message defaults; failures of a configured database are surfaced. The editor's text preview does not require changing the existing frame or CSP policies.

These changes are locally reviewed and tested with PGlite. They do not establish production readiness, apply migrations to Neon, or validate the deployed Cloudflare runtime. The production requirements above still apply.

## Local Phase 4b request follow-up

Create Your Stone uses admin-guarded explicit DTOs and strict quote/status action
inputs. Both writes use one conditional revision update; stale/overflowing inputs
fail closed. Database constraints bound cents, quantities, dimensions, statuses
and the required quote for non-New status. The customer FK restricts deletion.
Customer identifiers, specifications and image references are not mutable through
these actions. Seeded reference images are checked against the existing catalog
manifest. The separately approved public request/photo flow is documented below;
it does not allow arbitrary URLs or change existing request specifications.

Status labels are manual demo tracking only. Sending, messaging and payment are
disabled. Independent source review found a draft-loss path after status changes
under an active list filter; selection is now pinned independently of that filter,
with browser regression coverage. The editor retains its original revision across
new props and advances it only after confirmed saves. Real Neon and Worker behavior
remain separate release gates.

## Test shop checkout

`/{locale}/cart` is public; the cart lives in the browser (`localStorage`, `stone.cart.v1`) and is never
trusted. `quoteCart` is a public, read-only action (allow-listed in the guard scan): strict zod input of at
most 20 `{ slug, areaHundredths }` lines, published products only, no user id, no writes. `placeTestOrder`
guards first (`requireUser`), checks the configured origin like the request form, validates strictly,
re-prices on the server and refuses a total that differs from the one the customer confirmed
(`prices_changed` with the fresh quote). One SQL statement inserts the order and its items only when every
product is still published, the total still matches and the user has fewer than 50 test orders; a unique
`(user_id, idempotency_key)` index makes a retry return the same order (same key + other content =
`conflict`). No payment data is collected and no payment provider exists. The order page filters by the
session user, so another customer's number reads as a 404. A cart whose total would not fit the Postgres
`integer` cents column (2 147 483 647) is refused before the insert (`too_large`). The quote is one database
query whatever the cart size, and an order attempt about six (Workers allow 50 subrequests per request). The
browser cart is cleared once a sign-out is confirmed (shared devices).

Residual (accepted for the demo): the 50-order cap is a **soft demo limit**. It is counted inside the insert
statement but not serialised (each statement sees the order count at its start), so concurrent distinct
submissions by the same user near the limit can each pass and end above 50; there is no fixed bound on the
overshoot. It only limits demo data volume and is not a security or business quota. A strict quota would need a
serialised counter (e.g. a per-user row updated in the same statement, as the stone-request budget does).

Client retry key: `placeTestOrder` gets one idempotency key per submission, kept in memory for the page and
mirrored to sessionStorage (`src/features/cart/attempt-key.ts`). Retries in the same page view reuse it even when
storage is blocked or full; the key rotates after a success, a `conflict` or a changed cart. Limitation: with
storage unavailable, reloading the page after a lost response starts a new submission (any order saved by the
lost attempt is listed in the account's Orders).

## Public request/photo demo

`/ru/create-your-stone` and `/en/create-your-stone` require an existing session to
submit. The action guards first, explicitly checks the configured origin, parses
strict fields, derives ownership/status/number, and rate-limits attempts before
decoding. Preview/production requires an exact `BETTER_AUTH_URL` or `SITE_URL`;
the form is unavailable without it. Next's default 1 MiB action body limit remains.

The browser accepts JPEG/PNG/WebP up to 5 MiB and produces a PNG at most 512 px and
512 KiB. The server independently bounds signature, chunks, dimensions, bit depth,
color type, interlace, CRC and decoded scanlines; rejects animation/metadata/active
formats; and reencodes pixels only. Its public zlib preflight has a fixed 2 MiB
inflated-output cap and requires the exact scanline length. Other input and pixel
buffers also contribute to memory use. Streaming pngjs decode
avoids the private Node internals used by `PNG.sync.read`. No filename becomes a
path, and the original file is not retained. See the adversarial PNG tests and
local workerd probe in the public-request milestone report. Deployed CPU is unmeasured.

One SQL statement commits the private base64 PNG and request with atomic lifetime
demo limits: 50 new public requests total, 10 per owner. A database rate bucket
allows 10 attempts per minute per owner. Owner-scoped UUID plus canonical digest
deduplicates retries; even a concurrent repeat taking the last quota slot returns
the saved record. Browser recovery stores only that UUID, not contact details.

The photo route checks owner/admin before fetching bytes and returns `image/png`,
`private, no-store`, `nosniff`, same-origin resource policy and sandbox CSP. List
DTOs carry only a photo-present flag; image elements bypass the public optimizer.
Confirmation reads are also owner/admin-only. These are synthetic demo limits,
not a general file-storage service or a production moderation/retention policy.
The design follows the [OWASP upload guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html).

# STONE

Natural-stone demonstration website using Next.js, TypeScript and PostgreSQL, with Russian and English interfaces.

## Developer setup

Use Node 24.x and pnpm 12.11.2. Install with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`. Follow [development](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md) and [Node deployment](docs/NODE_DEPLOYMENT.md). Keep credentials in local/runtime configuration; never commit real values.

This is a review candidate derived from commit 6d8ce3cb6dd4e6ba9b9443e1963471b3e04e4067, with documentation and tooling-only export adjustments. It is not a production-ready release.

Catalog, calculator, account/admin, individual requests, cart and test checkout are implemented. No real payment or email delivery is provided. Reviews currently displays an empty state. Production Node uploaded-product-image storage is assigned to the receiving development team and requires its adapter.

Published source CI passed on 6d8ce3cb6dd4e6ba9b9443e1963471b3e04e4067: all six jobs, 1002 unit/integration tests and 682 browser tests; 115 conditional browser skips. [Developer handoff](docs/DEVELOPER_HANDOFF.md), [security](docs/SECURITY.md), [roles](docs/ROLES.md), [translations](docs/I18N.md) and [third-party notices](docs/THIRD_PARTY.md).

## Local quickstart with working authentication

Use a disposable local database and fictional accounts only. After the frozen dependency installation, create a new .env.local from .env.test.example; preserve any existing configuration. Set APP_ENV=development, PLATFORM=node, INDEXING=off, DATABASE_URL=pglite://.data/pglite and BETTER_AUTH_URL=http://localhost:3000. Ensure the .data directory exists. Then run pnpm db:seed followed by pnpm dev --hostname 127.0.0.1. Open /ru or /en on that origin. The fake accounts in the example are for isolated local use only. Stop the server before seeding again; one process owns the PGlite directory.
